At the air −water interface, these bubbles form a foam that is enriched in PFAS, so separation and collapse of the foam results in a concentrated foamate and a relatively PFAS- free retentate. 35 The process can be carried out in both batch and continuous operation. In continuous operation, stripping mode refers to operation with the liquid feed stream located above the liquid surface, whereas the feed enters below the foam/water interface in enriching mode. 35,36 Foam fractionation is a suitable water treatment technology for dilute solutions using only air, thereby eliminating the need for chemicals, solvents, ﬁlter material, and adsorbents. 37 Leachate water is a particularly complex matrix to treat, requiring extensive pretreatment before conventional PFAS treatment, such as GAC, ion exchange, or membrane ﬁltration, can be applied successfully. 29 These matrix e ﬀects are less problematic in the case of foam fractionation due to a beneﬁcial e ﬀect of high ionic strength on the process

Foam fractionation is a separation technology based on interfacial adsorption that selectively removes solutes according to their affinity for gas – liquid interfaces. It has shown promise in PFAS-contaminated water treatment due to its simple operation, high efficiency, and relatively low cost [15] . The process exploits the amphiphilic nature of PFAS, enabling their preferential accumulation at gas – liquid interfaces and subsequent separation via bubble flotation. However, PFAS concentrations in contaminated water typically range from ng ⋅ L � 1 to mg ⋅ L � 1 , far below the critical micelle concentration. Under such conditions, conventional foam fractionation suffers from low adsorption efficiency and poor foam stability, which hinder effective separation [16,17] . Introducing sur - factants can promote foam generation and enhance PFAS migration to interfaces. Landfills represent the primary endpoint for disposal of PFAS-laden waste, where, several years after landfilling, PFAS have leached and dissipated to the surrounding envi - ronments via landfill leachate ( Li et al., 2023 ). Numerous reports have highlighted the association between PFAS and health effects such as elevated cholesterol levels, increased cancer risks, diminished organ functions, and reproduction issues ( Sunderland et al., 2019 ). It leads to a range of regulations imposed on landfill leachate to restrict PFAS discharge into the environment. Foam fractionation is an adsorptive bubble separation technology that can remove surface‐active or amphiphilic contaminants from aqueous solutions in an aeration column due to their tendency to adsorb to gas‐ liquid interfaces that form a bubbl y liquid or foam. By removing the bubbly liquid or foam, the concentration of contaminant can be significantly reduced. Foam fractionation is a conspicuously sustainable method of removing per ‐ and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) because it requires no absorbent media or chemical amendments, and energy consumption is low. The process, which has been shown to be effective for the removal of a variety of surface ‐active contaminants, was arguably pioneered in its modern form by Lemlich and Lavi ( 1961), although its commercial adoption was , until recently, disappointing. It was with the recent explosion of concern to remediate PFAS ‐ contaminated water streams that interest in commercial exploitation of foam fractionation has grown. Foam fractionation (FF) is a physiochemical process in which hydrophobic and surface-active molecules are prefer - entially separated from aqueous solution via extraction by rising bubbles that form a foam layer at the aqueous surface. FF has been proven as a potent remediation technology for various types of wastewaters ( Eldib, 1961; Liu, 2013; Huang, 2017; Jia, 2021), and can be operated at all scales. It has the advantages of relatively simple equipment require - ment, low operation cost and energy consumption, and no need of re - agents addition. FF produces a small volume of highly-concentrated PFAS-containing solution that can be disposed or further treated ( Wong, 2001; Backleh-Sohrt, 2005).
